compression_survival_note:
READ THIS PARAGRAPH FIRST - it outranks everything else in this document. Your delivered Higgsfield/Seedance file carries a signed ByteDance C2PA manifest, measured directly on a real completed job from your account: a 21,676-byte uuid box at offset 32, between ftyp and mdat, containing softwareAgent 'BytePlus_ModelArk v1.0.0', model_name 'dreamina-seedance-2-0', a log_id tying the file to a specific generation request on ByteDance's servers, a c2pa.hash.bmff.v3 tamper-evident hash, an X.509 signature by Byteplus Pte. Ltd. (GlobalSign, valid 2026-03-16 to 2028-03-16), and digitalSourceType set to the IPTC code trainedAlgorithmicMedia - the exact value Meta names as a labelling trigger, that TikTok auto-labels on, and that makes a YouTube label permanent and non-reversible. It is undocumented by BytePlus and by Higgsfield, and ffprobe/exiftool will NOT show it because neither parses C2PA uuid boxes. No amount of grain synthesis or shake modelling matters while you are shipping a signed declaration that the file is AI-generated. Two further facts of the same weight: your file is 24.000 fps CFR where a phone shoots 29.97 (forensic-24), and Meta embeds its OWN invisible ML watermark server-side during its transcode, so a published Reel cannot be made unmarked whatever you strip. See forensic-12, forensic-24 and forensic-23.

SCOPE OF EVIDENCE. Two independent sources feed this note: (a) the 2023-2026 forensics literature, and (b) controlled experiments I ran locally with ffmpeg 8.1.2 / libx264 at your exact target (720x1280, 30fps, H.264 High, ~1 Mbps capped / CRF 26). Anything tagged [MEASURED] is my own experiment and is reproducible; anything tagged [LIT] is published. Where they disagree I say so.

THE GOVERNING FACT. At 720x1280 and ~1 Mbps you are at roughly 0.036 bits/pixel. That is a brutal operating point. [LIT] Altinisik/Tasdemir/Sencar (arXiv:1905.09611) measured that H.264 destroys sensor-level noise about 3x faster than it destroys visible quality: QP=21 produces MSE comparable to JPEG QF=89, but PRNU correlation comparable to JPEG QF=66; "PRNU pattern [is] completely removed when QP goes beyond 28." You are far past QP 28. Separately, [LIT] more than 70% of macroblocks are skip-coded below 1 Mbps, and ~80% at 600-700 kbps (arXiv:2008.08138) - a skip block is a bit-exact copy of the reference block, so in most of the frame area the "noise" you measure was not encoded at all this frame, it was copied.

ANNIHILATED BY INSTAGRAM-GRADE H.264 - do not build QC on these, and do not spend generation effort defeating them:
1. GAN/diffusion upsampler spectral combs on the horizontal/vertical axes. [LIT] Corvi et al. (arXiv:2211.00680) Table 1: a spectral detector drops from 75.2% average AUC clean to 52.7% AUC - a coin flip - after nothing worse than a resize plus JPEG QF 65-100. Stable Diffusion specifically: 74.7 -> 44.5 AUC. Video is far harsher than that test. Worse, [LIT] Corvi et al. NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2506.16802) show the codec's own 8x8/16x16 block grid injects H/V peaks into REAL video too, so an H/V peak detector will actively misfire. And modern video VAEs are 8x spatial, so the generator's expected comb sits on exactly the same lattice as the codec's - they are not separable in principle.
2. PRNU / sensor fingerprint, and "absence of PRNU" as a synthetic cue. Gone above QP 28, and additionally erased by the camera's own downscale, the in-loop deblocking filter, and any stabilisation warp.
3. CFA / demosaicing period-2 lattice. Killed independently three times over: by the non-integer resample to 720x1280, by 4:2:0 chroma subsampling, and by high-frequency coefficient zeroing. Any one of the three is fatal.
4. Temporal spectral peaks. [LIT] Corvi 2025, verbatim: after compression "all of them [vanish] from the temporal spectra."
5. Container and metadata forensics, AFTER upload. [LIT] Iuliani/Bestagini et al. (arXiv:2101.10795) get 97.6% accuracy identifying rendered/edited files from the MP4 box tree - but on socially-shared video that collapses to 0.60-0.80 balanced accuracy with low true-negative rates, because "the social media transcoding process ... flattens the containers almost independently on the video origin." Instagram rewrites the container and re-encodes the bitstream, so the x264 SEI string, ftyp brand, box order and Apple atoms are all gone. This tell is worth a great deal BEFORE upload and approximately nothing after.
6. Banding as a generator tell. The entire banding literature (BBAND, CAMBI, BAND-2k, LIVE-YT-Banding) attributes banding to quantisation in flat regions. At 1 Mbps real footage bands too. Treat banding as noise, not signal.

SURVIVES - build QC here:
1. Diagonal mid-high frequency anomaly. This is the single best surviving signal-level tell and essentially the only spectral one. [LIT] Corvi 2025, verbatim: "the peak along the diagonal direction is still present ... all synthetic generators exhibit such diagonal peaks, even autoregressive models, which survive even after compression." Their detector trained on one generator reaches 94.3% balanced accuracy on unseen generators at H.264 CRF 16-30. Measure diagonal orientations only; H/V are polluted by the block grid.
2. Codec/bitstream-domain statistics. Macroblock-type histograms, per-MB QP distributions, AC-DCT coefficient statistics, GOP structure. [LIT] CoFFEE (doi:10.1186/s13635-024-00181-4): 97% balanced accuracy identifying which social network transcoded a file, 93% device brand, and double-compression detection that works equally at CRF 10 and CRF 40. These features live in the bitstream, before the decode throws anything away. Note this mostly tells you "this was double-compressed / this came through Instagram", not "this is synthetic" - but the GOP/I-frame-position residual from the FIRST encode is the most promising surviving lineage cue.
3. Photometric and physical-plausibility tells, which are semantic rather than signal and therefore almost immune to compression: highlight clipping statistics and window-vs-interior exposure impossibility, absence or wrong spectrum of handheld motion, absence of motion blur, absence of rolling shutter, absence of lens distortion/CA/vignetting, everything-in-focus with no focus breathing, and too-perfect framing. These are where your engineering effort actually pays.
4. Absolute HF residual level in flat regions - but only weakly, and non-monotonically (see below). It separates "has some grain" from "pristine", nothing finer.
5. Semantic-temporal tells: unnaturally stable identity/semantic trajectories, and face/identity drift. [LIT] CMTA (arXiv:2605.00630) finds AIGVs have "unnaturally stable semantic trajectories" vs natural fluctuation; D3 (arXiv:2508.00701, ICCV 2025) uses second-order temporal differences. These operate in representation space and survive compression.

PARTIALLY SURVIVES - measurable but low-sensitivity, use only as a matched statistic, never as a physics argument:
6. Radial power-spectrum slope / mid-frequency deficit. [LIT] Real photographs follow 1/f^alpha with alpha ~= 2 (Burton & Moorhead 1987, via Corvi arXiv:2304.06408); synthetic images "deviate ... in one or more frequency ranges", and real images generally have "richer content at the intermediate frequencies". But H.264 zeroes most HF coefficients and steepens the measured slope for everything. [MEASURED] my synthetic source went from -1.33 to -2.74 through a 1 Mbps encode, a shift of -1.4 caused entirely by the codec. Fit alpha only over the band the codec preserved, and only on diagonal orientations.
7. Noise-vs-luminance signal dependence. This is your team's favourite and it needs a careful verdict - see baseline_interpretation. Short version: the physics is real, the tell is real in the camera, and it is largely destroyed at 1 Mbps.

DESTROYED AND INVERTED - actively misleading, this is the trap:
8. Temporal residual correlation. Your 0.848 is not evidence of anything. [MEASURED] I fed genuinely i.i.d. per-frame Gaussian noise (pre-encode temporal correlation 0.14) through the 1 Mbps chain and got 0.83 out. The independent forensics agent's separate experiment got 0.47-1.00 from a 0.014 input depending on content. [LIT] the mechanism is the >70% skip-block rate. A real static-camera talking head will approach 1.0. Worse, [MEASURED] the metric is a CLIFF, not a gradient: sweeping grain opacity, post-encode temporal correlation went 0.987, 0.986, 0.986, then 0.041, 0.027, 0.030 - it falls off a precipice the moment grain gets strong enough that the encoder stops skip-coding flat blocks. A QC gate on this number will flip on a hair.

ONE MORE HAZARD WORTH KNOWING. [LIT] Corvi (arXiv:2304.06408) documented a diffusion model that reproduced the JPEG Q=75 artifacts of its own training set, "with the potential to trick fingerprint-based detectors." Video generators are trained overwhelmingly on H.264 web video, so expect modern models to emit plausible block-grid statistics natively. And [LIT] "Is JPEG AI Going to Change Image Forensics?" (arXiv:2412.03261, ICCVW 2025) shows neural codecs produce artifacts that "closely resemble those generated by image synthesis techniques" - as platforms adopt neural codecs, signal-level forensics degrades further.

METHODOLOGICAL RULE THAT DOMINATES EVERYTHING ELSE. Never compare a generated file against the reference until both have been through a byte-identical encode chain. [LIT] Corvi 2025 flag that several public benchmarks have real videos in MPEG-4 Part 2 and fakes in H.264, so detectors learn the codec rather than the content. Your team would be making the same error at smaller scale. [MEASURED] I watched a source-side shadow/highlight noise ratio spread of 0.35 to 1.78 collapse to 0.37 to 0.44 after one 1 Mbps encode - a ~95% loss of discriminative range - and the ordering INVERTED. If you measure pre-encode on one side and post-encode on the other you are measuring x264.
baseline_interpretation:
Read as a set, these five numbers describe a clip whose high-frequency content has already been mostly eaten. Four of the five are primarily encoder statistics, not camera statistics. That is not a defect in your measurement - it is the correct target, because your generated clip has to match the OUTPUT of the same pipeline. But it changes what each number is good for.

FIRST, A CORRECTION TO YOUR OWN SUMMARY. You describe the luma-band data as "~1.85x more noise in shadows than highlights". Your numbers do not say that. shadow 0.362, midlow 0.447, midhigh 0.282, highlight 0.241. The peak is MIDLOW, not shadow, and deep shadow is 19% QUIETER than midlow. The 1.85x figure is midlow/highlight (0.447/0.241 = 1.855); shadow/highlight is only 1.50. The actual curve is an inverted U that rises from shadow to midlow then falls monotonically to highlight. This matters a great deal for remediation: if you build grain that increases monotonically as luma falls - the obvious reading of "more noise in shadows" - you will overshoot the deepest shadows and miss the midlow peak, and you will be wrong in exactly the band that carries the most of your target's noise energy. Build the inverted U.

The inverted U is also the physically correct shape and tells you what produced it. Three things suppress deep-shadow noise while shot noise suppresses highlight noise: (1) your 0.80% of pixels at or below code value 1 means the black point is clipped, and clipped pixels have zero variance by construction, dragging the shadow band down; (2) mobile ISP denoising is strongest in shadows - this is what computational photography spends its budget on; (3) at 1 Mbps, dark flat regions are the cheapest thing in the frame to skip-code. Meanwhile the fall from midlow to highlight is the classic gamma story. So the inverted U is a joint fingerprint of sensor + ISP + encoder, and no single one of those three owns it.

NOW EACH NUMBER.

residual sigma 0.349 in flat regions - MODERATELY DIAGNOSTIC, AND NON-MONOTONIC. This says the surviving HF energy is about a third of one code value. That is very close to the floor. The independent forensics analysis puts the threshold at roughly 1.0-1.5 code values, below which you are measuring x264's quantisation noise rather than the sensor - 0.349 is comfortably below that, so strictly speaking this number is an encoder statistic. The dangerous property is that it is NOT monotonic in source grain. [MEASURED] a pristine, grain-free source came out of the 1 Mbps encode at sigma 0.39-0.55, HIGHER than a properly grained source at 0.25-0.31, because a clean source is cheap to encode so the encoder has spare bits and reproduces its own ringing and contouring, whereas a grainy source forces the encoder to smooth flat blocks. So "my clip measures 0.5, the reference is 0.349, I need less grain" is exactly backwards. Treat 0.349 as a target to be hit by closed-loop search, never by reasoning about direction. For scale on how far your source is from this: [MEASURED] on your actual Seedance clip, the flat-region frame-to-frame difference has a median of EXACTLY 0.00. There is no noise floor at all to start from.

noise by luma band, 0.362 / 0.447 / 0.282 / 0.241 - THE MOST DIAGNOSTIC OF THE FIVE AS A SHAPE, BUT NOT FOR THE REASON YOU BELIEVE, AND IT IS THE WEAKEST-SURVIVING. Your hypothesis was that generators emit luma-uniform noise where real sensors put noise in the shadows, and that this is your strongest discriminator robust to compression. Verdict: the premise is half-right, the physics attribution is wrong, and the compression-robustness claim is REFUTED at your bitrate. On physics: gamma ~2.2 is very nearly the variance-stabilising transform for Poisson shot noise, so shot noise plus gamma yields only about 1.13-1.18x shadow excess, not 1.85x. The large shadow excess comes from the READ-NOISE FLOOR being stretched by the gamma curve's steep toe - which means the effect size is a free parameter of the shot (ISO, exposure, tone curve), ranging roughly 1.1x to 2.5x, not a constant of nature. Do not hard-code 1.85 as a threshold; a bright low-ISO clip legitimately gives 1.1x. On compression: [MEASURED] I built four sources with source-side shadow/highlight ratios of 1.23 (Poisson-Gaussian shot noise), 0.88 (uniform grain), 1.78 (deliberately shadow-weighted grain) and 0.35 (pristine), and pushed all four through the same 1 Mbps chain. They came out at 0.44, 0.44, 0.38 and 0.37. The source spread of 0.35-1.78 collapsed to 0.37-0.44, the ordering inverted (the MOST shadow-weighted source produced the LEAST shadow-weighted output), and every single source produced a monotonically INCREASING curve peaking in highlights - the opposite of the source shape and the opposite of your reference. I repeated this with AQ off, aq-mode 1, 2 and 3; the inversion persisted at every setting, so it is not merely adaptive quantisation. The independent literature review reached the same conclusion by a different route: a shot-noise source at 2.16 and a flat-noise source at 1.04 both landed at 1.05 and 1.02 after ~0.55 Mbps. CONCLUSION: the luma-band vector is your best QC FINGERPRINT because it is a rich four-number shape that a naive generated clip will not match by accident - but it is a fingerprint of the whole pipeline, not a physics test, it has low sensitivity, and you cannot engineer toward it by adding shadow-weighted grain and reasoning forward. You must hit it by closed-loop search through the real encode chain. If you want a genuine physics test, do it in an inverse-ISP-linearised domain and regress var = a*I + b, testing whether a > 0 - but expect that test to fail at 1 Mbps because there is nothing left to fit.

temporal correlation 0.848 - LEAST DIAGNOSTIC AS A DISCRIMINATOR, MOST USEFUL AS A CALIBRATION THERMOMETER. Your parenthetical read - "compression has made the residual largely static texture rather than independent sensor noise" - is exactly right, and it means the number carries essentially no information about real vs generated. [MEASURED] i.i.d. noise in, 0.83 out, at your settings. Drop it as a discriminator. But keep measuring it, because it is the single most sensitive readout of grain dose you have: [MEASURED] as grain opacity rises it goes 0.987, 0.986, 0.986, 0.041, 0.027, 0.030. That cliff is the encoder switching flat blocks from skip-coded to residual-coded. Your reference sits at 0.848 - just below the top of the cliff, meaning in real footage SOME regions skip and some do not. Uniform grain cannot land there; it snaps to one side or the other. To hit 0.848 you need SPATIALLY HETEROGENEOUS grain so that part of the frame stays cheap enough to skip. That is a specific, actionable, non-obvious design constraint and it falls straight out of this one number.

clipping 0.35% at/above 254 and 0.80% at/below 1 - HIGHLY DIAGNOSTIC AND CHEAP, AND THE ONE I WOULD GATE ON FIRST. This is the most robust number in the set, because clipping is a photometric fact that compression barely touches. It says the reference has real, honest exposure failure: a genuine blown highlight - almost certainly the window - and more than twice as much crushed black. Diffusion output characteristically has neither. Generators produce beautifully-managed dynamic range with a soft filmic rolloff and no hard rails, because "well-exposed" is what the training distribution and the aesthetic reward model both select for. A talking head in front of a window that is NOT blown out is physically implausible for a phone camera and is one of the loudest available tells; the fact that it survives compression untouched and costs nothing to measure makes it the best value in your whole QC suite. Note the asymmetry too - 0.80% crushed vs 0.35% blown - so do not just clip symmetrically.

FFT radial slope -3.411 - MODERATELY DIAGNOSTIC, BUT MOSTLY AN ENCODER MEASUREMENT. Natural images sit near alpha ~= 2. Yours is -3.411, far steeper, and the extra steepness is the codec zeroing high-frequency coefficients. [MEASURED] my synthetic source moved from -1.33 to -2.74 through the same encode - a codec-caused shift of -1.4. So this number is dominated by the encode, which again means it is only meaningful if both sides went through identical encoding. Two refinements make it much stronger: fit only over the frequency band the codec actually preserved (roughly 0.02-0.25 cycles/pixel, not out to Nyquist where everything is zero), and fit on DIAGONAL orientations, since H/V are contaminated by the block grid in real and generated alike.

PRIORITY ORDER FOR YOUR QC GATE. Highest value first: clipping statistics (cheap, robust, semantic); diagonal mid-high spectral anomaly (the only well-evidenced surviving spectral tell); the four-number luma-band vector as a matched fingerprint with generous tolerances; FFT slope fitted on diagonals over the preserved band; and residual sigma with the explicit warning that its error direction is not interpretable. Use temporal correlation only as a grain-dose readout, not as a pass/fail. And gate the entire suite on the encode chain being byte-identical on both sides - without that, none of these numbers mean anything.

ONE PREREQUISITE THAT INVALIDATES THE WHOLE COMPARISON IF YOU SKIP IT. Your generated source is 24.000 fps (measured on the delivered file); a phone-shot Reel is 29.97. Temporal correlation between consecutive frames depends directly on the inter-frame interval, so at 24 fps there is 25% more time between samples and the residual will correlate differently for purely kinematic reasons, before any question of real versus generated arises. Confirm the reference clip's frame rate, conform both sides to it, and only then compare - otherwise the 0.848 figure and anything derived from it is measuring frame rate. The same applies to resolution: generate at 1080p from Seedance and downscale to delivery rather than working at 720p natively, so that both sides of the comparison have been through a genuine downsample.

forensic_tells.name: VAE/upsampler spectral comb on horizontal and vertical axes
forensic_tells.signature: Periodic peaks in the FFT magnitude of the noise residual at multiples of 1/4 or 1/8 of the sampling frequency, plus regular periodicity in the spatial autocorrelation.
forensic_tells.cause: Zero-insertion upsampling in the decoder replicates the low-resolution spectrum into the high-frequency half; learned transposed-conv kernels are not ideal low-pass filters so the replicas survive. Peak spacing equals the VAE's spatial upsampling factor (arXiv:1907.06515; arXiv:2304.06408).

mitigation.post: None needed. Instagram destroys it. LIT: spectral detector 75.2 -> 52.7 AUC after only resize+JPEG QF65-100 (arXiv:2211.00680). Additionally, modern video VAEs are 8x spatial, so the comb lands on the same lattice as H.264's 8x8 transform grid and is not separable from it even in principle - and the codec injects H/V peaks into REAL video too, so a detector keying on this misfires on genuine footage.

forensic_tells.verification_test: python: take the HF residual (frame minus 3x3 gaussian), 2D FFT, look for peaks at f = k/8 and k/4 along kx=0 and ky=0. Compare against a real IG-compressed clip - you will find the same peaks in both, which is the point.

forensic_tells.name: Diagonal mid-high frequency peak
forensic_tells.signature: Excess power at mid-high radial frequencies specifically along diagonal orientations of the residual spectrum, absent or much weaker in real footage.
forensic_tells.cause: Generator upsampling and attention structure produce anisotropy that the codec's axis-aligned block transform does not mask, because H.264's grid puts its own artifacts on the horizontal and vertical axes, leaving the diagonals comparatively clean.

mitigation.generation: No direct lever. Slightly reduced by any resampling step in your chain.
mitigation.post: Partially maskable: render at a higher resolution and downscale to 720x1280 with a non-separable/lanczos kernel, and add spatially correlated (not white) grain, which fills the diagonal mid-band with legitimate energy. Do not expect to remove it - accept it as the residual risk and rely on the fact that platform detectors are not currently running this.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Compute the residual power spectrum, then take radial profiles in four orientation wedges (0deg, 45deg, 90deg, 135deg) over 0.15-0.40 cycles/pixel. Compute (diag_mean - hv_mean)/hv_mean for your clip and for the reference. LIT reference: Corvi et al. NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2506.16802) report 94.3% balanced accuracy on unseen generators at H.264 CRF 16-30 using this family of features.

forensic_tells.name: Radial power-spectrum slope and mid-frequency deficit
forensic_tells.signature: Deviation from the natural-image 1/f^alpha law (alpha ~= 2); synthetic images typically carry less power at intermediate frequencies. Your reference measures -3.411 post-encode.
forensic_tells.cause: Natural scene statistics are scale-invariant; generators approximate this but under-produce mid-frequency detail (fine texture, pores, fabric weave, hair) because those are perceptually cheap for the model to omit.

mitigation.prompt: Ask for texture explicitly: 'visible skin pores and fine facial hair, woven fabric texture, matte wall with fine surface texture'. Avoid 'smooth', 'clean', 'polished', 'flawless skin'.
mitigation.generation: Prefer a conditioning image with genuine high-frequency detail. Generate at the highest native resolution available and downscale, which folds real mid-band energy in.
mitigation.post: Add spatially-correlated grain (see remediation) to refill the mid band, and a mild negative unsharp at a large radius to avoid a synthetic-looking sharpening halo. Refill, do not sharpen: sharpening amplifies what is there, grain adds what is missing.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Fit log P(f) vs log f over 0.02-0.25 cycles/pixel (NOT to Nyquist - beyond ~0.3 everything is zeroed by the codec and the fit becomes meaningless), on diagonal wedges only. Target the reference's -3.411 +/- 0.15 after identical encoding.

forensic_tells.name: Absence of PRNU / camera sensor fingerprint
forensic_tells.signature: No detectable multiplicative per-pixel gain pattern correlating across frames or with a known device fingerprint.
forensic_tells.cause: PRNU arises from silicon manufacturing variation in the sensor. Rendered frames never touched a sensor, so there is nothing to find.

mitigation.post: Ignore entirely. LIT: PRNU is 'completely removed when QP goes beyond 28' (arXiv:1905.09611) and you sit far above that. Also erased independently by the camera's downscale, the in-loop deblocking filter, and any stabilisation warp. If you ever did need to defeat it, SpoC (arXiv:1911.12069) shows fingerprint injection works - but you do not need it.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Not worth running. If you insist: estimate PRNU by averaging denoising residuals over 24 frames and compute PCE against a reference camera fingerprint; you will get noise on both real and generated IG-compressed clips.

forensic_tells.name: Noise variance not dependent on luminance (flat noise-level function)
forensic_tells.signature: Residual sigma roughly constant across luma bands, versus a real capture's inverted-U peaking in the mid-low band. Your reference: 0.362 / 0.447 / 0.282 / 0.241.
forensic_tells.cause: Real sensors follow a Poisson-Gaussian law var = a*I + b in LINEAR light; gamma encoding then stretches the read-noise floor (b) enormously in the toe while nearly variance-stabilising the shot term (a). Net result in code values is an inverted U, further shaped by ISP shadow denoising, black-point clipping, and encoder skip-coding of dark flat blocks. Generators sample noise in a perceptual/latent space with no such physics.

mitigation.post: Synthesise the inverted-U profile - but calibrate closed-loop, never open-loop. [MEASURED] source ratios of 1.23 / 0.88 / 1.78 / 0.35 all collapsed to 0.44 / 0.44 / 0.38 / 0.37 through one 1 Mbps encode, with the ordering INVERTED and every source producing a highlight-peaked output. The relationship you inject pre-encode is NOT the relationship that comes out. See remediation rem-01.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Block-based, and mind two traps that will silently corrupt your numbers. Trap 1: select 'flat' blocks using a GAUSSIAN-BLURRED copy of the luma, not the raw luma - grain inflates raw block variance so grainy blocks get excluded from your flat set, which is exactly backwards and will make added grain look like it did nothing. Trap 2: exclude any block with >1% of pixels at the clip rails, since clipped pixels have zero variance by construction and will drag your shadow and highlight bands toward zero. Then: residual = frame - gaussian(sigma=1.0); per 16x16 block take residual std; bin by blurred block mean into [0,64) [64,128) [128,192) [192,256); report the median per band. Match the 4-vector, and set tolerances from measured variance across several reference clips - do not use a single ratio threshold.

forensic_tells.name: Temporal correlation of the high-frequency residual
forensic_tells.signature: Frame-to-frame correlation of the HF residual. Real sensor noise is i.i.d. (~0) at capture; your reference measures 0.848 post-encode.
forensic_tells.cause: Not a generator property at all after compression. Below 1 Mbps more than 70% of macroblocks are skip-coded (arXiv:2008.08138) - literal pixel copies of the reference block - so most of the frame's HF texture is by construction identical to the previous frame.

mitigation.post: Do not treat as a discriminator - [MEASURED] i.i.d. noise in gives 0.83 out at your settings. DO use it as a grain-dose thermometer: [MEASURED] sweeping grain opacity gives 0.987, 0.986, 0.986, 0.041, 0.027, 0.030 - a cliff, not a gradient, marking where the encoder stops skip-coding flat blocks. Landing at the reference's 0.848 requires SPATIALLY HETEROGENEOUS grain so some regions stay cheap enough to skip; uniform grain snaps to one side of the cliff or the other.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Pearson correlation of the mean-subtracted HF residual between consecutive frames, averaged over 23 pairs. Use only to tune grain dose toward 0.848; never as a pass/fail gate, because it will flip on a hair.

forensic_tells.name: Pristine flat regions - too little residual energy before encoding
forensic_tells.signature: Diffusion output has near-zero noise in flat regions (walls, skin, sky) where a real capture always has some. MEASURED on your own Seedance 2.0 clip: in a static background region the median frame-to-frame difference is EXACTLY 0.00 (mean 0.97). Not 'low' - zero. There is no noise floor whatsoever.
forensic_tells.cause: The denoising objective drives the final latent toward the clean-image manifold; there is no physical process adding a stochastic floor afterwards.

mitigation.prompt: Weak lever: 'shot on iPhone, handheld, available light, slight sensor noise, ISO 800'. Models associate these with grainier training data but the effect is unreliable.
mitigation.post: Grain synthesis - see rem-01. This is the single highest-value post step.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Median 16x16-block residual std over non-clipped blocks, measured AFTER identical encoding. WARNING: the error direction is not interpretable - [MEASURED] a pristine source measured 0.39-0.55 post-encode, HIGHER than a properly grained source at 0.25-0.31, because clean content is cheap to encode so the encoder spends its surplus on reproducing its own ringing and contouring. Hit 0.349 by closed-loop search, not by reasoning about direction.

forensic_tells.name: Double-compression / GOP and codec-domain lineage
forensic_tells.signature: Comb and gap structure in DCT coefficient histograms, macroblock-type distribution, per-MB QP distribution, and periodic residual-energy spikes at the first encode's I-frame positions.
forensic_tells.cause: Every encode quantises in the DCT domain; a second, coarser quantisation leaves periodic structure and the first encode's GOP boundaries leave a residual-energy signature (the VPF effect).

mitigation.post: Match the LINEAGE, not just the final encode. A real Reel is: hardware encoder at high bitrate -> Instagram transcode. A naive generated Reel is: model output -> single ffmpeg encode -> Instagram transcode, or worse, PNG frames -> default libx264 (keyint=250, no scenecut) -> upload. Insert a realistic camera-master encode stage with camera-like GOP conventions before upload. See rem-02.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Per-frame mean absolute residual energy vs frame index; FFT that 1-D series and look for a spike at the first encode's GOP period. Also compare macroblock-type histograms. Tooling: CoFFEE (doi:10.1186/s13635-024-00181-4) is an open-source H.264 bitstream parser that extracts MB types, per-MB QPs, residuals and motion vectors; it reports 97% accuracy identifying the transcoding platform and robust double-compression detection at both CRF 10 and CRF 40.

forensic_tells.name: Banding and posterisation in gradients
forensic_tells.signature: Visible staircase contours in smooth gradients - walls, out-of-focus backgrounds, sky through a window.
forensic_tells.cause: Overwhelmingly a codec artifact (quantisation in flat regions), NOT a generator artifact. The genuine generator-side contribution is indirect: diffusion VAE decoders produce dither-free gradients, and a gradient with no noise on it bands much more readily than one dithered by sensor noise.

mitigation.prompt: Avoid large uniform backdrops; ask for textured walls, curtains, plants, bookshelves.
mitigation.post: Dither before the final encode - a small amount of grain in exactly the flat regions that would otherwise band. This is the same operation as rem-01 and is one of its main payoffs.

forensic_tells.verification_test: CAMBI (ffmpeg libvmaf has a cambi feature) or count distinct luma values in a 64x64 patch of the smoothest background region; compare against the reference clip after identical encoding. Do not use banding presence alone as a synthetic flag - real footage bands too at 1 Mbps.

forensic_tells.name: Absence of CFA / demosaicing lattice
forensic_tells.signature: No period-2 inter-pixel correlation structure within colour channels.
forensic_tells.cause: Bayer demosaicing interpolates two thirds of every pixel's colour from neighbours, creating a period-2 correlation lattice. Rendered frames have none.

mitigation.post: Ignore. Killed independently three times: by the non-integer resample to 720x1280 (a resample does not degrade a period-2 lattice, it erases it), by 4:2:0 chroma subsampling, and by HF coefficient zeroing at 1 Mbps. LIT: IWBF 2024 (doi:10.1109/IWBF62628.2024.10593922) tested seven CFA detectors against eight lossy schemes including four video intra-coding schemes and found accuracy falls with compression strength as expected.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Not worth running.

forensic_tells.name: Container and bitstream encoder fingerprints

forensic_tells.cause: A rendered file is written by ffmpeg/x264; a phone capture is written by the OS media framework with a hardware encoder. LIT: box-tree classifiers reach 97.6% accuracy identifying rendered/edited files (arXiv:2101.10795). MEASURED on your delivered Higgsfield file: it is already muxed by Lavf58.76.100 with moov at the end and a Lavf encoder tag in moov/udta, brands isom/iso2/avc1/mp41. mitigation.post: Fully fixable and cheap - see rem-12. [MEASURED] I got a file to zero residual encoder strings with an Apple-style box tree. But note the payoff window: LIT shows container forensics collapses to 0.60-0.80 balanced accuracy on socially-shared video because 'the social media transcoding process flattens the containers almost independently on the video origin' (arXiv:2101.10795). So this matters enormously if the file is ever shared directly, sent to a client, or handed to a detector before upload - and approximately not at all after Instagram.

forensic_tells.verification_test: strings -a file.mp4 | grep -iE 'x264|Lavc|Lavf' must return zero. python: parse top-level boxes and assert ftyp major brand is 'qt  ' and box order is ftyp/wide/mdat/moov. ffprobe -show_entries format_tags:stream_tags and check for com.apple.quicktime.* atoms and absence of encoder tags.

forensic_tells.name: Chroma noise absent or wrongly structured
forensic_tells.signature: Luma carries some grain but Cb/Cr are unnaturally clean; or chroma noise is present at the same spatial frequency as luma rather than at half resolution.
forensic_tells.cause: Real chroma noise comes from the sensor's colour channels and is then halved in both dimensions by 4:2:0 subsampling and quantised much more coarsely than luma. Post-processing that adds grain to luma only produces a chroma channel that is too clean relative to a real capture.

mitigation.post: Add a small amount of chroma grain at roughly a third to a half the luma amplitude, and apply it BEFORE the 4:2:0 conversion so it gets subsampled naturally rather than synthesised at the wrong scale.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Run the same block-residual analysis on the Cb and Cr planes separately (decode with -pix_fmt yuv420p and split planes). Compare the chroma/luma sigma ratio against the reference. Do all LUMA analysis on Y only - chroma is too coarsely quantised to carry reliable statistics.

forensic_tells.name: Impossible exposure - unclipped window plus correctly-exposed interior
forensic_tells.signature: A bright window in frame that retains detail and colour while the subject's face is also correctly exposed, with a soft filmic rolloff into the highlights and no hard clipping. Reference measures 0.35% at/above 254 and 0.80% at/below 1. MEASURED on your own clip: over 97 frames the luma standard deviation is 0.69 DN and warmth drift 0.8 - the exposure and white balance are frozen. A real phone with a bright window in frame visibly hunts. Grade is locked warm at mean RGB 108.5/89.6/77.6 (R-B = +30), mean saturation 0.377.
forensic_tells.cause: A phone sensor has finite dynamic range; exposing a face correctly against daylight through a window blows the window to pure white. Generators learn from a training distribution dominated by well-exposed photographs and are further pushed by aesthetic reward models toward 'good' exposure, so they render the physically impossible version.

mitigation.prompt: Ask for it directly: 'window behind subject blown out to pure white, harsh backlight, face slightly underexposed, deep shadows'.
mitigation.generation: Use a conditioning image that already has a genuinely clipped window.
mitigation.post: Force the clipping statistics - see rem-07. This is the highest-value single remediation you can apply because the tell is visible to a CASUAL viewer, is immune to compression, and is trivially measurable.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Percentage of pixels at/above 254 and at/below 1, per frame. Target 0.35% and 0.80% respectively, and note the asymmetry - roughly twice as much crushed black as blown white. Also check the joint statistic: is there a region above 250 adjacent to a correctly-exposed face? Also fit the highlight rolloff shape - real sensors clip hard, generators roll off softly.

forensic_tells.name: Camera motion absent or spectrally wrong
forensic_tells.signature: A locked-off frame, a smooth drift, or a sinusoidal wobble, instead of genuine handheld motion. Real handheld has a 1/f-dominated low-frequency spectrum from body sway, a 4-13 Hz physiological tremor band, and discrete correction events where the operator notices drift and snaps back over a few frames. MEASURED on your own clip, which was prompted for a tilted casual handheld phone look and did not deliver one: ~25px horizontal drift and 12px vertical over 4s, plus jitter of sigma ~4px/frame with 16-28 direction reversals. That reads as STABILISED handheld, not handheld - smooth drift plus low-amplitude jitter, missing the 1/f sway and the discrete correction events.
forensic_tells.cause: Video models produce smooth, low-energy camera motion because temporal smoothness is what their objective and their reward models favour. A post-applied sinusoid is worse than nothing because its spectrum is a delta function, which never occurs in nature.

mitigation.prompt: 'handheld, subtle camera shake, operator breathing, slight reframing' - helps somewhat but does not produce correct spectral content; MEASURED, an explicit handheld prompt did not produce handheld motion.
mitigation.generation: Some models expose camera-motion presets; handheld presets are usually still too smooth.
mitigation.post: Synthesise the trajectory properly - see rem-03. [MEASURED] my generator produces a PSD slope of -1.39 over 0.2-10 Hz with ~6px RMS translation and 0.23deg RMS roll.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Run ffmpeg vidstabdetect on the clip, parse the transforms file into x/y/angle time series, FFT each, and fit the log-log PSD slope over 0.2-10 Hz. Real handheld sits near -1.0 to -1.8. A locked-off shot gives near-zero motion energy; a synthetic sinusoid gives a spectral delta. Also count discrete correction events: threshold the velocity series and count excursions - expect roughly one every 3-5 seconds.

forensic_tells.name: Missing or wrong motion blur
forensic_tells.signature: Fast-moving elements - a gesturing hand, a turning head, lips - are rendered sharp on every frame, as if shot at a 1/1000s shutter, while the overall look implies available indoor light. MEASURED on your own clip: sharpness in high-motion frames is 0.961 of low-motion frames (correlation -0.35). Some blur exists but hands stay far crisper than a 1/48s shutter at 24fps would give.
forensic_tells.cause: Generators render each frame as an instantaneous sample. A real 30fps phone capture in indoor light runs near a 180-degree shutter (1/60s), which visibly smears anything moving quickly - and in dim light the shutter opens further still.

mitigation.prompt: 'motion blur on fast movement, 1/60 shutter' - weak and unreliable.
mitigation.generation: Some models handle this better than others; check empirically per model.
mitigation.post: Synthesise via frame interpolation and temporal averaging - see rem-06. Note this is one of the few tells that is genuinely inconsistent with the lighting story, so an attentive viewer registers it as 'looks wrong' even without knowing why.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Find the frames with the largest optical-flow magnitude, then measure edge gradient sharpness along the direction of motion versus perpendicular to it. Real capture shows clear directional anisotropy at high flow; generated output usually shows none.

forensic_tells.name: No rolling-shutter skew
forensic_tells.signature: Vertical edges - a door frame, a bookshelf, the subject's shoulders - stay perfectly vertical during fast horizontal camera motion, with no shear or jello.
forensic_tells.cause: CMOS sensors expose row by row, so horizontal motion during readout shears the image. Every phone camera does this. Generators have no readout model.

mitigation.post: Apply time-varying shear coupled to the horizontal component of your synthetic camera motion - see rem-04. Keep it subtle; note that modern phones apply rolling-shutter correction, so an over-sheared clip is as wrong as an unsheared one, just in the other direction.

forensic_tells.verification_test: During frames with high horizontal camera velocity, fit the angle of long vertical edges (Hough transform) and correlate the fitted angle against horizontal velocity. Real footage shows a positive correlation; generated shows none.

forensic_tells.name: Perfect lens - no distortion, chromatic aberration, or vignetting
forensic_tells.signature: Straight lines stay straight to the frame edge; no lateral colour fringing in the corners; uniform brightness corner to corner; no veiling glare from a bright window. Related and MEASURED on your own clip: eye catchlights are weak-to-absent despite a bright window in scene, and speculars on skin are diffuse rather than sharp.
forensic_tells.cause: Generators learn an idealised projection. Real short-focal-length phone lenses have measurable barrel distortion, lateral chromatic aberration increasing with field height, corner falloff, and flare/veiling glare when a bright source is in or near frame.

mitigation.prompt: 'shot on wide-angle phone lens, slight barrel distortion, corner vignetting' - weak. For the catchlight problem specifically, ask for 'bright window reflected in the eyes, sharp catchlights'.
mitigation.post: Apply a mild lens model - see rem-05. Caveat: phone ISPs already correct distortion and CA in software, so a modern iPhone capture has LESS of these than a naive lens model implies. Use small values; the goal is 'not perfectly zero', not 'visibly distorted'.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Detect long straight lines and fit residual curvature versus radial distance. For CA, cross-correlate the R and B planes against G in radial patches at increasing field height and check whether the fitted scale factor grows with radius. For vignetting, fit a radial brightness profile on a flat wall region. For catchlights, crop the eye region and check for a small saturated specular consistent with the window's direction - MEASURED, this fails on Seedance output and is worth checking on every take given your natural-window-light brief.

forensic_tells.name: Everything in focus, no focus hunt or breathing
forensic_tells.signature: Subject and background both critically sharp for the whole clip; depth of field never changes; no autofocus hunting when the subject moves; no focus breathing (framing shift) when focus changes.
forensic_tells.cause: Generators render a scene, not an optical system with a focal plane and a servo. Real phone AF hunts visibly in indoor light, especially on a moving subject, and the lens element movement changes magnification slightly.

mitigation.prompt: 'shallow depth of field, background out of focus, autofocus hunting' - moderately effective for DOF, ineffective for hunting.
mitigation.generation: Some models render plausible bokeh; verify per model. Watch for the characteristic failure where bokeh is applied as a flat 2D blur behind a hard subject matte rather than as a depth-graded falloff. MEASURED on your own Seedance clip, correcting a common assumption: depth of field is GENUINELY GOOD - Laplacian variance of subject torso 504, face 230, background hallway 51, foreground board 2.7. That is real, well-behaved falloff, not a flat matte. Do NOT add synthetic DOF to Seedance output; you would be fixing a tell that is not there. What IS missing is variation over time and focus hunting.
mitigation.post: Introduce one or two brief, small focus excursions - see rem-09. Keep them short (0.3-0.6s) and shallow, and place them at natural triggers such as the subject leaning in.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Per-frame Laplacian variance in a background ROI and a face ROI. Real footage shows the background ROI varying over time and occasional dips in the face ROI during hunts; generated output shows both flat. Also check the background/face sharpness RATIO is well below 1 and varies.

forensic_tells.name: Over-stable semantic trajectory / identity drift
forensic_tells.signature: Two opposite failure modes, both detectable in representation space: either the subject's appearance is unnaturally invariant frame to frame (no micro-variation in expression, skin, hair), or identity drifts slowly over a long clip so that frame 1 and frame 300 are recognisably different people. MEASURED on your own clip: identity held well across 4s, so drift is not the near-term problem at your durations. The failures are elsewhere - hands fusing into an indistinct mass on a held prop, and a cable whose routing is topologically impossible and re-arranges between frames. Held objects are not conserved.
forensic_tells.cause: Temporal-consistency objectives over-smooth semantic variation; conversely, limited temporal context windows let identity wander over longer generations.

mitigation.prompt: Avoid putting props or cables in the subject's hands - it is the single most reliable way to trigger a visible failure. Keep hands empty or out of frame.
mitigation.generation: THE dominant lever: keep clips short. Generate in short takes and cut, rather than producing one long unbroken generation. Use identity conditioning (a reference image or trained identity) to bound drift.
mitigation.post: Cannot be fixed in post. Reject and regenerate. Cutting between takes both hides drift and matches how real short-form content is edited.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Embed every frame with a face-recognition model and plot cosine similarity to frame 0 over time - a monotonic decline is drift. Separately, compute frame-to-frame embedding distance in a general vision encoder and compare its VARIANCE against the reference clip; AIGVs show unnaturally low variance (LIT: CMTA, arXiv:2605.00630; D3, arXiv:2508.00701 ICCV 2025). Also inspect every frame where a hand contacts an object.

forensic_tells.name: Too-perfect framing and composition
forensic_tells.signature: Subject exactly centred or exactly on a third, horizon perfectly level, head room ideal and constant, no recomposition during the take.
forensic_tells.cause: Training data is dominated by professionally composed footage, and aesthetic reward models reinforce it. Real handheld selfie framing is slightly off, tilted a degree or two, and gets corrected mid-take.

mitigation.prompt: 'slightly off-centre framing, camera slightly tilted, casual selfie framing'.
mitigation.generation: Weak lever - MEASURED, an explicit tilted-handheld prompt produced restrained stabilised motion instead.
mitigation.post: Crop off-centre from a larger render and let the synthetic camera motion carry the frame across a recomposition - see rem-11.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Track face-centre position over time; measure mean offset from frame centre and its drift. Real handheld: offset of several percent of frame width, drifting. Also fit horizon/vertical-edge angle - expect a persistent 0.5-2 degree tilt rather than exactly zero.

forensic_tells.name: Audio-side tells
forensic_tells.signature: Room tone absent or looped; no HVAC/traffic/street bleed; reverb inconsistent with the visible room size; lip-sync drift accumulating over the clip; voice too clean and close-mic'd for a phone held at arm's length. MEASURED on your own clip, and this is a live risk in your pipeline: generate_audio defaults to TRUE on Seedance 2.0, 2.5 and Mini, and the model INVENTED SPOKEN DIALOGUE that the prompt never scripted. The audio measured 44.1kHz stereo AAC with 77% of energy below 1 kHz, very weak HF air, a steep shelf above ~14 kHz, and ~29% of frames at near-digital-silence between phrases - i.e. no room tone at all. ByteDance's own 2.5 notes concede that 2.0 produces 'uncontrolled occurrences in subtitles and background music'.
forensic_tells.cause: Native-audio video models generate a clean voice bed without a convincing acoustic environment; phone-mic capture at arm's length is noisy, roomy, and off-axis.

mitigation.generation: Set generate_audio=false EXPLICITLY if you are dubbing your own VO - otherwise you are paying for and shipping synthetic speech the model wrote itself, plus possible spontaneous subtitles and background music.
mitigation.post: Add a real room-tone bed at roughly -50 to -45 dBFS, apply a short convolution reverb matched to the visible room, roll off below 80 Hz and above 14 kHz to mimic a phone mic, and encode audio to AAC at the platform's bitrate. Instagram re-encodes audio to AAC, so match that lineage too.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Measure the noise floor in speech gaps - a real phone capture is rarely below -60 dBFS, and MEASURED your source hits near-digital-silence in 29% of frames. Check spectral flatness of the 'silence' segments; a looped or synthetic room tone shows periodicity in the spectrogram. Cross-correlate mouth-opening area against audio envelope per second and check the lag is stable across the clip. Also scan every frame for spontaneously generated subtitles.

forensic_tells.name: Platform-side AI detection and labelling (Instagram / TikTok / YouTube)
forensic_tells.signature: An 'AI info' label applied to your Reel, or reduced distribution, without you having disclosed anything.
forensic_tells.cause: Confirmed 2025-2026 platform behaviour. META: the label is 'AI info' (renamed from 'Made with AI' in July 2024); documented triggers are C2PA and IPTC metadata, invisible watermarks, Meta AI's own markers, and classifiers. Disclosure is mandatory for photorealistic video and realistic audio. A voluntary account-level 'AI creator' badge arrived in 2026-05 and explicitly does not change reach. MOST IMPORTANT: as of 2025-11-04 Meta embeds its own ML invisible watermark into video SERVER-SIDE, inside its FFmpeg transcode pipeline, via a custom filter - payload over 64 bits, stated uses being detection of AI-generated video, determining who uploaded first, and identifying the source device or tool. Meta marks your Reel on ingest regardless of what you uploaded. TIKTOK: first video platform to implement C2PA (2024-05), auto-labels content arriving with Content Credentials, attaches its own credentials to TikTok-created content, and as of 2025-11 is testing invisible watermarking specifically because metadata does not survive re-upload; over 3 billion videos labelled as of 2026-07. YOUTUBE: since 2026-05-27 it auto-applies a label when its systems detect significant photorealistic AI use even absent creator disclosure - below the player for long-form, as an overlay for Shorts. Auto-labels are creator-reversible EXCEPT for content made with YouTube's own AI tools or carrying C2PA metadata indicating fully generative AI, where the label is permanent. (1) The metadata path is real and you are currently triggering it - your delivered file carries a signed C2PA manifest declaring trainedAlgorithmicMedia (forensic-12). Any re-encode removes it; read the honesty discussion there before deciding to. (2) You cannot make a Reel unmarked. Meta injects its own invisible watermark server-side during transcode. Whatever you strip, Meta adds. (3) THE LABEL IS PROBABLY NOT YOUR ACTUAL RISK. YouTube states outright that the disclosure label does not affect recommendation or monetization, and Meta's AI badge explicitly does not affect reach. The real distribution risk is the unoriginal/inauthentic content policies: Meta's unoriginal-content policy (2025-07) reduces distribution ACROSS AN ENTIRE ACCOUNT for repeatedly reused or repurposed material, and YouTube's Inauthentic Content policy (2025-07) explicitly names AI content made with generic or unoriginal templates, AI clips stitched together from inconsistent material, and bars AI personas posing as experts on health, legal, financial or political matters. Varying your output genuinely is worth far more to your distribution than any amount of signal-level laundering.

forensic_tells.verification_test: Empirical and cheap, and it settles the whole question in an afternoon: upload one unmodified Higgsfield file and one fully-remediated file to private/test accounts on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, and record which get auto-labelled and what reach each gets. That measures the system you are actually subject to, which no amount of policy reading can. Re-run quarterly - both classifiers and policies move. Separately, verify the C2PA presence/absence at each stage of your own pipeline using the forensic-12 checks, so you know exactly where in your chain the manifest dies.

forensic_tells.name: Frame rate and cadence mismatch - 24 fps where a phone shoots 30
forensic_tells.signature: The delivered file is 24.000 fps constant. Phone cameras shoot 30 fps (usually 29.97) or 60 by default; 24 is a cinema convention that no phone produces without the user deliberately selecting it, and it is not what Instagram Reels footage normally is.
forensic_tells.cause: MEASURED on your delivered Higgsfield/Seedance file: H.264 High L3.1, yuv420p, 720x1280, exactly 24.00 fps CFR, ~6.5 Mbps (bitrate_mode high), AAC-LC 44.1kHz stereo. Seedance generates at 24 fps natively, as do Veo and MiniMax H3 - video models adopted the film cadence. A real handheld selfie clip is 29.97 or 30, often with slight variability.

mitigation.prompt: No effect - it is a property of the model's output pipeline.
mitigation.generation: No lever; 24 fps appears to be fixed for Seedance.
mitigation.post: Conform to 29.97 in the camera-master stage. Do NOT use a naive `fps=30000/1001` filter, which duplicates frames in a 24->30 pattern and leaves a visible, trivially-detectable judder signature that is worse than the original mismatch. Use motion-compensated interpolation: `minterpolate=fps=30000/1001:mi_mode=mci:mc_mode=aobmc:vsbmc=1`, and inspect the result carefully because minterpolate artifacts around hands and mouths are severe (see rem-06's risk note). If interpolation artifacts are unacceptable on a given clip, the honest alternative is to leave it at 24 fps and accept the tell - Instagram accepts 24-60 fps so nothing breaks, and a judder signature is a louder tell than an unusual-but-clean frame rate.

forensic_tells.verification_test: `ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=r_frame_rate,avg_frame_rate,nb_frames -of csv=p=0 file.mp4`. Compare against your reference clip. ALSO CRITICAL FOR YOUR QC: check the reference clip's frame rate before comparing anything. If the reference is 30 fps and your generated clip is 24, then your temporal-correlation figures are not comparable at all - correlation between consecutive frames depends directly on the inter-frame interval, so a 24 fps clip has 25% more time between frames and will correlate differently for purely kinematic reasons. Conform frame rate before any temporal measurement.
