remediation_playbook.technique: Closed-loop QC harness - build this FIRST, before any other remediation
remediation_playbook.how:
Every other item in this playbook is calibrated through this harness, so it is not optional infrastructure - it is the method. The rule: NEVER compare a generated clip to the reference until both have been through a byte-identical encode chain. [MEASURED] a source-side shadow/highlight noise ratio spread of 0.35-1.78 collapsed to 0.37-0.44 after one 1 Mbps encode and the ordering inverted; without matched encoding you are measuring x264, not content.
Implementation: (a) an analyse(clip) function returning the 5-metric vector; (b) an encode_lineage(clip) function implementing rem-02; (c) a sweep driver that varies ONE remediation parameter, runs generated->lineage->analyse, and reports distance to the reference vector.
The analyser, with the two traps that will silently corrupt your numbers if you miss them:
  residual = frame - gaussian_filter(frame, sigma=1.0)   # HF residual
  TRAP 1: select flat blocks using a GAUSSIAN-BLURRED copy of luma, never raw luma. Grain inflates raw block variance, so grainy blocks get excluded from your 'flat' set - which means added grain appears to do nothing and you will chase your tail. I hit this exact bug mid-analysis and it inverted my conclusions until fixed.
  TRAP 2: exclude any 16x16 block with >1% of pixels at the clip rails (>=253 or <=2). Clipped pixels have zero variance by construction and will drag your shadow and highlight bands toward zero, producing meaningless ratios (I got a 'ratio' of 2044 and one of 1.3e13 before adding this guard).
  Then: per 16x16 block take residual std; bin by blurred block mean into [0,64)/[64,128)/[128,192)/[192,256); report median per band, plus overall median, plus temporal correlation, clipping percentages, and the diagonal-wedge FFT slope over 0.02-0.25 cycles/pixel.
Distance metric: normalise each of the 5 metrics by the standard deviation you measure ACROSS SEVERAL reference clips (not one), then use a weighted L2. Weight clipping highest, temporal correlation lowest or zero.
Critical: measure the reference variance across at least 5-10 real clips before setting any tolerance. A single reference clip gives you a point, not a distribution, and you will end up over-fitting to one shot's lighting.
remediation_playbook.risk: Over-fitting to a single reference clip is the main danger - you will tune your whole pipeline to one room's lighting and one subject's wardrobe. Also beware treating the metric vector as a target to be minimised to zero: real clips differ from each other by a substantial margin, so a generated clip that matches the reference EXACTLY is itself anomalous. Aim to land inside the real-clip cloud, not on its centroid.

remediation_playbook.technique: Encode-lineage matching - a camera-master stage before the platform transcode
remediation_playbook.how:
A real Reel has been through two encoders: the phone's hardware encoder at high bitrate, then Instagram's transcode. A naive generated Reel has been through one, or worse, through libx264 defaults (keyint=250, no scenecut) which no camera on earth produces. Insert a camera-master stage.
THREE CORRECTIONS FROM MEASURING YOUR ACTUAL DELIVERED FILE, which is 720x1280, H.264 High L3.1, 24.000 fps CFR, ~6.5 Mbps, AAC-LC 44.1 kHz, muxed by Lavf58.76.100 with moov at end:
  (a) FRAME RATE. Your source is 24 fps; a phone shoots 29.97. Conform in this stage - see forensic-24 for the method and its risks. Every sendcmd timing in this playbook assumes you have settled on a frame rate first; regenerate the shake and AE command files at whatever rate you conform to.
  (b) RESOLUTION. Generate at 1080p from Seedance (2.0 goes to 4K, 2.5 to 1080p) rather than 720p, so the downscale to delivery is a genuine downsample that folds in real mid-band energy, rather than an upscale that invents it. Meta recommends 1080x1920 for Reels.
  (c) AUDIO. Your source is 44.1 kHz; Meta's Reels spec asks for 48 kHz, so resample yourself rather than letting Meta do it. Meta also specifies AAC-LC at 128 kbps or better, stereo, 4:2:0 chroma, and a closed GOP of 2-5 seconds.

Stage 1, camera master (approximates an iPhone H.264 capture - iPhones default to HEVC, so this models the 'Most Compatible' setting; for HEVC use libx265 here and let Instagram convert):
  ffmpeg -i generated.mp4 -vf "scale=1080:1920:flags=lanczos" \
    -c:v libx264 -profile:v high -level 4.2 -preset slow \
    -b:v 16M -maxrate 20M -bufsize 24M \
    -x264-params "keyint=30:min-keyint=30:scenecut=0:bframes=0:ref=1:aq-mode=1" \
    -pix_fmt yuv420p -color_primaries bt709 -color_trc bt709 -colorspace bt709 \
    -r 30000/1001 -c:a aac -b:a 192k -ar 48000 -ac 2 master.mp4
  The GOP conventions matter more than the bitrate: hardware camera encoders use a short fixed GOP (~1s), no scene-cut detection, no B-frames, single reference. That combination is a camera signature and libx264 defaults are its opposite. [MEASURED] this produced 15.9 Mbps.
  Note 30000/1001 (29.97) rather than exactly 30 - phone captures are 29.97 or variable, exact-30 CFR is a render signature.
Stage 2, the Instagram-side transcode, applied IDENTICALLY to both your clip and the reference for QC purposes:
  ffmpeg -i master.mp4 -vf "scale=720:1280:flags=bicubic" \
    -c:v libx264 -profile:v high -level 3.1 -preset medium \
    -crf 26 -maxrate 1100k -bufsize 2200k \
    -x264-params "keyint=60:min-keyint=30:scenecut=40:bframes=3:ref=3:aq-mode=1:aq-strength=1.0" \
    -pix_fmt yuv420p -color_primaries bt709 -color_trc bt709 -colorspace bt709 \
    -c:a aac -b:a 128k -ar 44100 ig_sim.mp4
  [MEASURED] this produced 1.27 Mbps, in the right neighbourhood for your ~1 Mbps reference.
IMPORTANT CALIBRATION STEP: these Stage 2 parameters are my reconstruction. Meta publishes an INPUT spec (mp4, H.264/H.265, AAC-LC 128kbps+ 48kHz stereo, 9:16, 1080x1920 recommended and 540x960 minimum, 24-60 fps fixed progressive, 4:2:0, closed GOP 2-5s, 3-90s) but publishes NO output ladder - no target bitrate, no resolution ladder. Widely-repeated figures for what Instagram delivers could not be confirmed against any primary source, so do not trust them, including mine. Calibrate by taking a clip you control, uploading it, downloading the processed version, and tuning Stage 2 until its metric vector matches. Until you do that you are simulating a guess.
What you upload is the Stage 1 master, at the platform's recommended spec - do NOT pre-compress to 1 Mbps yourself, since that would stack three encodes instead of two.
remediation_playbook.risk: Getting Stage 2 wrong is worse than not simulating it, because every downstream calibration inherits the error. Uploading an over-compressed file stacks an extra generation of loss and visibly degrades quality. Setting bframes=0 in Stage 1 costs bitrate efficiency, which is fine at 16 Mbps but would be wasteful if you lowered it. Also: if Instagram ever switches your content to HEVC or AV1 delivery, this whole lineage model needs redoing.

remediation_playbook.technique: Grain synthesis with an inverted-U luma profile and spatial heterogeneity
remediation_playbook.how:
Build the inverted U your reference actually shows (shadow 0.362, midlow 0.447 PEAK, midhigh 0.282, highlight 0.241), not a monotonic shadow ramp. A monotonic ramp overshoots deep shadows and misses the midlow peak where most of the target's noise energy lives. Note your starting point is not 'a little grain' - [MEASURED] your Seedance source has a flat-region frame-to-frame median difference of exactly 0.00.
Fast, validated chain - one blend with the weight derived from the pixel's own luma, no mask plumbing. [MEASURED] 6.6x realtime at 720x1280, i.e. ~3 min for a 30s clip:
  ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -f lavfi -i "nullsrc=s=720x1280:r=30" -filter_complex \
   "[1:v]format=gray,noise=alls=40:allf=t+u,format=yuv420p[g]; \
    [0:v][g]blend=all_expr='A+(B-128)*(K*(0.35+2.6*(A/255)*pow(1-A/255,1.7)))'" \
   -c:v libx264 -crf 10 -pix_fmt yuv420p grained.mp4
  The weight term 0.35+2.6*(A/255)*(1-A/255)^1.7 is an asymmetric hump. [MEASURED] I evaluated it against your reference profile: it peaks at luma 94 (inside your midlow band, which is where your reference peaks), and its band-mean ratios relative to the highlight band are shadow 1.38, midlow 1.83, midhigh 1.53, highlight 1.00 - against your reference's 1.50 / 1.855 / 1.17 / 1.00. The midlow peak matches to within 2% and the shadow band to within 8%; midhigh runs high, so if you want a closer fit raise the exponent from 1.7 toward 2.1, which pulls the curve down faster above the peak. K is your single calibration scalar and does not change the shape. The expression is syntax-validated and runs.
Alternatives by cost: blend=all_mode=grainmerge:all_opacity=X is [MEASURED] 1.8x realtime but gives a FLAT profile (no luma weighting); geq is [MEASURED] 4.4x realtime and allows arbitrary per-channel expressions but is fiddly to escape. The blend_expr form above is the best trade.
SPATIAL HETEROGENEITY IS MANDATORY, and this is the non-obvious part. [MEASURED] uniform grain makes post-encode temporal correlation snap between 0.986 and 0.041 as opacity crosses a threshold - it is a cliff, because the encoder flips flat blocks between skip-coded and residual-coded all at once. Your reference sits at 0.848, i.e. PARTWAY, which is only reachable if some regions of the frame stay cheap enough to skip while others do not. Multiply the grain by a slowly-varying low-frequency field so the dose differs across the frame:
  add to the chain: perlin=s=720x1280:r=30,format=gray,gblur=sigma=40 as a third input, and multiply it into the weight.
Chroma: apply grain BEFORE the 4:2:0 conversion at roughly a third of the luma amplitude so it gets subsampled naturally (forensic-13).
CALIBRATION - do this, do not guess. [MEASURED] on my test scene, sweeping K gave post-encode sigma_flat of 0.357 / 0.328 / 0.310 / 0.308 / 0.274 / 0.252 for opacities 0.03 / 0.05 / 0.07 / 0.10 / 0.15 / 0.22 - note it DECREASES as you add more grain, because the encoder responds by smoothing harder. The value that hit the 0.349 target was the SMALLEST one tested. Your scene will differ; run the sweep.
remediation_playbook.risk: Two failure modes, in opposite directions. Too much grain: the encoder spends its bitrate on your synthetic noise instead of on the subject's face, so the clip looks mushy AND post-encode residual measures LOWER than the target - the metric moves the wrong way and you will be tempted to add still more, which makes it worse. Too little: banding returns in gradients and flat regions read as synthetic. Also, grain that is white (uncorrelated) rather than spatially correlated fills the wrong part of the spectrum and will push your FFT slope away from target - use a slightly blurred grain plate, not pure per-pixel noise. Finally, never add grain AFTER your final encode.

remediation_playbook.technique: Handheld camera shake with correct spectral content
remediation_playbook.how:
The spectrum is the whole point. Real handheld = 1/f-dominated body sway + a 4-13 Hz physiological tremor band + discrete correction events. A sinusoid is a spectral delta and reads as fake; a smooth drift has no tremor band - and [MEASURED] smooth drift plus low-amplitude jitter is exactly what Seedance gives you even when explicitly prompted for handheld.
Generate the trajectory offline and drive ffmpeg with sendcmd (validated end to end):
  1. Synthesise x(t), y(t), roll(t) in numpy: build 1/f^1.6 noise by shaping white noise in the Fourier domain (amplitude f^-0.8, random phase, irfft); add a separately band-passed 4-13 Hz component at ~20-25% of the sway amplitude; then inject discrete correction events - pick random times, add a step of ~0.7x the sway RMS, and smooth each step over 3-8 frames so it reads as a deliberate hand correction rather than a jump. One event every 3-5 seconds.
  2. Write a sendcmd script, one line per frame:
     0.0333 crop x 19.15, crop y 14.83, rotate angle -0.00636;
  3. Apply, rendering from a padded source so the crop always has material:
     ffmpeg -i padded_760x1352.mp4 -vf \
       "sendcmd=f=shake.cmd,crop=720:1280:20:36,rotate=angle=0:fillcolor=none:bilinear=1" \
       -c:v libx264 -crf 10 -pix_fmt yuv420p shaken.mp4
[MEASURED] my generator at pad=14px produced x_rms 5.79px, y_rms 6.41px, roll_rms 0.235deg, and a PSD slope of -1.39 over 0.2-10 Hz - squarely in the real-handheld range, versus your source's smooth-drift signature.
Scale to context: a seated talking head at arm's length is toward the low end (3-6px RMS at 720x1280); walking-and-talking is several times more. Roll should be present but small - 0.15-0.35deg RMS. Translation and roll should be partially correlated, since a real wrist rotates as it translates.
Generate the padded source by rendering at 760x1352 (or upscaling your 720x1280 output with lanczos, accepting the softness cost, which the grain stage then partly masks). Better still, generate at 1080p and downscale to 760x1352 so the pad costs you nothing.
remediation_playbook.risk: Over-amplitude is the obvious failure - it reads as a shaky-cam affectation rather than an unremarkable handheld take, and it destroys the 'natural window light talking head' register. Subtler and more damaging: motion costs bitrate. At 1 Mbps every pixel of global motion forces the encoder to code motion vectors and residual across the whole frame instead of skip-coding the background, so aggressive shake measurably degrades quality and will push your residual metrics around. It also fights any stabilisation Instagram or the viewer's player might apply. And if you crop-and-rotate without enough pad you will expose black edges, which is an instant giveaway.

remediation_playbook.technique: Rolling-shutter shear coupled to horizontal camera velocity
remediation_playbook.how:
Derive the shear from the SAME trajectory that drives the shake, so the two are physically consistent - shear that is uncorrelated with camera motion is worse than no shear.
  shx(t) = C * dx/dt   where dx/dt is horizontal velocity in px/frame and C is a small constant.
Write it into the same sendcmd file and add shear to the chain (validated):
  printf "0.0 shear shx 0.000;\n0.5 shear shx 0.006;\n1.0 shear shx -0.004;\n" > rs.cmd
  ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "sendcmd=f=rs.cmd,shear=shx=0:shy=0:fillcolor=none" ...
Magnitude: keep peak |shx| in the 0.002-0.008 range. At 720x1280 an shx of 0.006 displaces the top and bottom rows by roughly +/-4px relative to centre, which is perceptible only on long vertical edges - correct.
Sign convention: for a camera panning right, the bottom of the frame (read last) lags, so verticals lean. Check the direction empirically against a real clip rather than reasoning it out; readout order varies by sensor orientation and the front camera is often mirrored.
remediation_playbook.risk: Modern phones apply rolling-shutter correction in the ISP, so a real 2026 iPhone capture has noticeably LESS skew than a naive CMOS model predicts. Over-shearing is therefore doubly wrong - it is both visible as jello and inconsistent with a modern capture. If your reference clip shows no measurable skew, skip this entirely; adding it would create a mismatch rather than fix one. This is a low-severity tell (2/5) and I would implement it last, if at all.

remediation_playbook.technique: Lens model - barrel distortion, lateral chromatic aberration, vignetting, veiling glare
remediation_playbook.how:
All four validated. Apply BEFORE the shake crop so the distortion is anchored to the lens, not to the moving frame - this ordering matters and getting it backwards produces distortion that swims around, which is its own tell.
Barrel distortion:
  lenscorrection=k1=-0.028:k2=0.004:i=bilinear
  Negative k1 barrels. Phone ultra-wides run stronger; the main camera after ISP correction is nearly rectilinear, so stay small.
Lateral chromatic aberration - scale R up and B down slightly so fringing grows with field height (validated; note the setsar=1 calls, without which mergeplanes fails on a SAR mismatch):
  -filter_complex "[0:v]format=gbrp,split=3[r0][g0][b0]; \
    [r0]extractplanes=r,scale=iw*1.0020:ih*1.0020,crop=720:1280,setsar=1[r]; \
    [g0]extractplanes=g,setsar=1[g]; \
    [b0]extractplanes=b,scale=iw*0.9986:ih*0.9986,pad=720:1280:(ow-iw)/2:(oh-ih)/2,setsar=1[b]; \
    [r][g][b]mergeplanes=0x001020:gbrp,format=yuv420p"
  Scale factors of 1.002/0.9986 give sub-pixel fringing at centre growing to ~1.5px at the corners - about right. A cheaper approximation is chromashift=cbh=1:crh=-1 but it applies a constant shift rather than a radial one, so it is less faithful.
Vignetting:
  vignette=angle=PI/7:mode=forward   (mild corner falloff; larger angle = stronger)
Veiling glare from the window (validated) - real lenses scatter light from a bright source across the whole frame, lifting blacks:
  -filter_complex "[0:v]split[a][b];[b]gblur=sigma=60,eq=brightness=0.02[bl]; \
     [a][bl]blend=all_mode=screen:all_opacity=0.07"
  This is one of the more valuable items here because it directly attacks the 'impossibly clean interior next to a bright window' look, and it lifts your deep shadows, which interacts with the clipping targets in rem-07.
remediation_playbook.risk: Phone ISPs already correct distortion and CA, so over-application makes the clip look like it came from an uncorrected action cam - a different kind of wrong. Vignetting is the easiest to overdo and reads instantly as an Instagram filter from 2013. Veiling glare over-applied washes out contrast and will move your clipping statistics: it raises the floor, reducing your at-or-below-1 percentage, so re-check rem-07 after tuning it. Also, the CA chain resamples all three planes, which costs sharpness.

remediation_playbook.how:
NOTE ON FRAME RATE: the numbers below assume a 30 fps timeline. Your Seedance source is 24 fps (forensic-24), where a 180-degree shutter is 1/48s rather than 1/60s - i.e. genuinely MORE blur per frame. Settle your frame rate via rem-02 before tuning this, and scale the intermediate fps accordingly (for 24 fps use fps=96 with tmix=frames=2 for a true 180 degrees).
Interpolate to a higher frame rate, average groups of frames, then decimate - this synthesises true vector blur rather than a directionless smear. Validated:
  ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf \
    "minterpolate=fps=120:mi_mode=mci:mc_mode=aobmc:vsbmc=1,tmix=frames=3:weights='1 1 1',fps=30" \
    -c:v libx264 -crf 10 -pix_fmt yuv420p blurred.mp4
  At 120fps intermediate and tmix over 3 of the 4 sub-frames you get a 3/4 duty cycle - slightly wider than a 180-degree (1/2) shutter, which suits indoor available light where the shutter genuinely opens further. For a true 180 degrees use fps=120 with tmix=frames=2.
  Cheap fallback if minterpolate is too slow or artifacts on your content: tmix=frames=2:weights='1 1' straight on the source. Cruder, but fast and better than nothing.
Target: [MEASURED] your source's high-motion/low-motion sharpness ratio is 0.961; a real 1/48s shutter would put it substantially lower. Measure the ratio after this step and tune the duty cycle to close the gap.
Apply AFTER the shake so camera motion contributes to the blur (physically correct), and BEFORE the grain, so grain does not get temporally averaged into mush. If you are also conforming 24->29.97 (forensic-24), do both in one minterpolate pass rather than two.
remediation_playbook.risk: minterpolate is the most artifact-prone filter in this entire playbook. On fast hand gestures, occlusion boundaries, and around the mouth it produces warping and tearing that is far more damaging than the missing motion blur it fixes - and those artifacts look exactly like AI generation artifacts, so you would be manufacturing the very tell you are trying to remove. This is especially dangerous on Seedance output, where hands on props already fail (forensic-20). Inspect every clip at full resolution after this step. If the subject gestures quickly, use the tmix fallback or skip it. Over-wide duty cycles smear lips and wreck perceived lip-sync.

remediation_playbook.technique: Highlight clipping and shadow crush to defeat the impossible-exposure tell
remediation_playbook.how:
This is the highest-value item in the playbook: the tell is visible to a CASUAL viewer, is completely immune to compression, and is trivially measurable. Targets from the reference: 0.35% of pixels at/above 254 and 0.80% at/below 1 - note the asymmetry, roughly twice as much crushed black as blown white.
Best fix is upstream. In the prompt, ask for it: 'window behind subject blown out to pure white, strong backlight, face slightly underexposed, deep shadows in the corners of the room'. Generators resist this because their aesthetic priors favour balanced exposure - and Seedance's documented default is 'floaty, overlit' - so verify per clip rather than assuming.
In post, to FORCE clipping rather than tame it, push exposure on the window region and let it rail. For a stationary window, build a soft elliptical mask and lift only that region:
    -filter_complex "[0:v]split[a][b];[b]eq=brightness=0.35:contrast=1.25[hot]; \
      [0:v]format=gray,geq=lum='255*exp(-((X-500)^2/40000+(Y-300)^2/90000))',format=yuv420p[m]; \
      [a][hot][m]maskedmerge"
Then crush the black point, asymmetrically larger than the highlight push:
    colorlevels=rimin=0.012:gimin=0.012:bimin=0.012
and iterate the two constants until the measured percentages land on 0.35% / 0.80%.
A validated tone curve for the surrounding grade - note this is a ROLLOFF and shapes the shoulder, it does not itself create clipping; use it alongside the region lift, not instead of it:
  curves=master='0/0.004 0.18/0.176 0.5/0.5 0.78/0.802 0.9/0.918 0.97/0.962 1/0.978'
  It lifts the very bottom slightly (0/0.004) to model veiling glare and is near-linear through the mids.
Measure after the full lineage, not before - the encode shifts both percentages slightly (in my runs 0.459% -> 0.438% at the top).
remediation_playbook.risk: Clipping is destructive and irreversible - you are throwing away real image data to buy realism, and if you overshoot, the window becomes a featureless white slab and faces lose modelling in the shadows. Crushing blacks too hard is the more common error and it eats the shadow detail that your grain work in rem-01 depends on: a crushed region has zero variance, so it drops out of your flat-block analysis entirely and will skew the shadow band. Also, hard clipping creates large flat regions which the encoder loves to skip-code, pushing temporal correlation up. Re-measure the whole vector after tuning this, not just the clipping numbers.

Overdone, this looks like a broken grade or a pumping auto-exposure on a cheap webcam - and pumping is itself a strong 'something is wrong' signal. Drift that is periodic (a slow sine) is worse than none, for the same spectral reason as the shake. Large gamma moves will shift your luma-band histogram and therefore your entire noise-vs-luma vector, so re-measure. Also, if you apply AE drift after grain, you scale the grain along with the image and decorrelate it from the luma profile you calibrated - apply drift BEFORE grain.

remediation_playbook.technique: Focus hunt (but NOT synthetic depth of field)
remediation_playbook.risk: Too-frequent or too-deep hunting reads as a malfunctioning camera and is distracting in a talking-head where the viewer is watching the face - you are degrading the thing the audience came for. A global blur also softens the already-soft background, which can look like a double-blur. Blur reduces high-frequency content and will move your FFT slope and residual sigma, so run the QC harness after adding it. If the reference clip's subject is critically sharp throughout, do not add hunting at all.

remediation_playbook.how:
A real phone lens is smudged. The key property, and the reason this is a good tell to exploit, is that the smudge is fixed to the LENS, not the scene - so it stays put while the frame moves underneath it. Nothing in a generated clip does that, and it is a strong positive signal of physical camera-ness.
Validated chain - blur a copy and merge it through a soft blob mask, applied AFTER the shake crop so the smudge stays frame-locked while content moves:
  -filter_complex "[0:v]split[a][b];[b]gblur=sigma=9[s]; \
     [0:v]format=gray,geq=lum='120*exp(-((X-500)*(X-500)/40000+(Y-300)*(Y-300)/90000))',format=yuv420p[m]; \
     [a][s][m]maskedmerge"
  Place the blob toward a corner or edge, never over the face. Peak mask value of ~120/255 gives a partial blend - a subtle haze, not a visible fingerprint. Combine with the veiling-glare step from rem-05 for a smudge that also blooms when the window is behind it, which is exactly what a real greasy lens does.
Use ONE blob, and keep it in the same place across every clip in a batch if they are meant to be the same phone - consistency across clips is itself a realism signal.
remediation_playbook.risk: Over-strength turns into an obvious vaseline patch. Placing it anywhere near the face costs you the only thing the viewer is looking at. Because it is frame-locked and static, it is also perfectly compressible - a large static soft region is cheap for the encoder and will pull temporal correlation up, so check that metric after adding it. This technique is low-severity and I would treat it as polish, not priority.

remediation_playbook.how:
Render larger than delivery and crop off-centre, then let the shake trajectory carry a slow recomposition across the take. Validated:
  scale=760:1352:flags=lanczos,crop=720:1280:26:52
  The crop offsets 26 and 52 are deliberately not the centred values (20 and 36) - that is the point. Vary them per clip.
Add a persistent small tilt: rotate=angle=0.012 (about 0.7 degrees) held for the whole clip, on top of the roll variation from the shake. Real handheld selfie framing is rarely level and the tilt persists rather than averaging out. [MEASURED] prompting Seedance for a tilted casual look did not produce one, so this has to be done in post.
For recomposition, add a slow ramp to the crop x/y in your shake sendcmd file - the operator drifts off over 4-6s then corrects. This is already what the 'discrete correction events' in rem-03 produce; just make one of them larger and place it mid-clip.
Head-room: aim for the subject's eyeline slightly off the upper third and a horizontal offset of 3-8% of frame width, varying per clip.
remediation_playbook.risk: Cropping from 760x1352 to 720x1280 costs a small amount of resolution and the upscale-then-downscale round trip softens the image - acceptable, and partly masked by grain, but it stacks with the softening from rem-06 and rem-09 so watch the total. Generating at 1080p (rem-02) removes this cost entirely. Overdone offset or tilt looks like a mistake rather than casual framing, and in vertical short-form the subject drifting too far off-centre fights the format's conventions and can hurt watch-through. Also, if you crop off-centre you must ensure your shake pad still has material on the tighter side.

remediation_playbook.how:
PRECONDITION - read forensic-12 first. Your delivered file carries a signed BytePlus C2PA manifest declaring the content as trainedAlgorithmicMedia. Everything below removes it as a side effect. That is a deliberate choice with legal and disclosure dimensions, not a neutral technical cleanup, and it should be made explicitly with whoever owns legal.

With that said, the technical picture. Your source file is ALREADY muxed by FFmpeg (Lavf58.76.100, moov at end, brands isom/iso2/avc1/mp41), so you are inheriting a render fingerprint rather than creating one. Three separate fingerprints must be handled; removing only the obvious one leaves the other two.
1. The x264 SEI user-data string is embedded in the H.264 BITSTREAM, not the container, and lists every encoder option - it survives remuxing and -fflags +bitexact does NOT remove it. Strip the SEI NAL units (type 6):
     -bsf:v "filter_units=remove_types=6"
2. The container-level encoder tags (encoder=Lavc..., format-level Lavf...):
     -fflags +bitexact -flags:v +bitexact -map_metadata -1 -map_metadata:s:v -1
3. The box structure and brand. Use -f mov, which yields ftyp major brand 'qt  ' and an Apple-style box order. Critically, do NOT use +faststart - it moves moov before mdat, which is a render signature; cameras write mdat first.
Full validated command:
  ffmpeg -i master.mp4 -c copy -f mov \
    -bsf:v "filter_units=remove_types=6" \
    -fflags +bitexact -flags:v +bitexact -map_metadata -1 -map_metadata:s:v -1 \
    -metadata:s:v handler_name="Core Media Video" \
    -movflags "+use_metadata_tags" out.mov
[MEASURED] result: zero residual encoder strings; ftyp major brand 'qt  '; box order ftyp/wide/mdat/moov - the iPhone pattern. One residue I could not remove through ffmpeg alone: stream tag vendor_id=FFMP, which would need a hex patch of the stsd box.
I have deliberately OMITTED the com.apple.quicktime.make/model/software atoms from the command above - see the risk note.
Apply the SEI strip at ENCODE time on the master, then remux. HONEST SCOPE: this is worth ~0 after Instagram's transcode, which rewrites everything - and Meta additionally injects its own ML invisible watermark server-side during that transcode. So you cannot make a published Reel unmarked; you can only control what the file says before it gets there. Container work matters when the file is shared directly, delivered to a client, or examined before upload.
remediation_playbook.risk: Steps 1 and 2 merely remove information about your own toolchain and are unobjectionable. Step 3's optional Apple atoms are different: writing com.apple.quicktime.make=Apple and a model string is a deliberate misattribution to a real company's product, and it is the one item in this playbook with a downside beyond quality. If these files are ever presented as authentic camera captures to a platform, an advertiser, or in any context where provenance is relied on, forged Apple capture metadata turns a stylistic choice into a misrepresentation. I would strip the ffmpeg fingerprints and stop there. Technically: -c copy with a bitstream filter can fail on some streams; verify the output decodes. And an inconsistent file - metadata stripped but C2PA left, or vice versa - is more anomalous than either alone.

remediation_playbook.how:
The strongest lever you have, and it costs nothing. Nearly every model-side failure - identity drift, hand morphing, physics violations, lip-sync drift, background instability - is a function of duration. Generate in short takes and cut, rather than asking for one long unbroken generation.
Practical policy for a 4-30s Reel: generate in takes at or below the model's reliable coherence length, then assemble. Cuts are free realism in this format - real short-form talking-head content is heavily cut, so a 25s single unbroken take is itself unusual, while three cuts is unremarkable.
Place cuts at natural speech boundaries, and vary shot size slightly across takes (a small push-in or a different crop from rem-11) so the cuts read as deliberate edits.
Benefit for QC: a cut resets identity drift, resets accumulated lip-sync error, and gives the encoder an I-frame at a natural point, which is what real edited content produces.
CALIBRATION DATA for Seedance: the API allows 30s on 2.5 but that is not the coherent length. A 95-minute feature on this stack reported ~15s of usable footage per attempt and a 64:1 reroll ratio (16,181 generations for 253 shots) with ~3,000-word prompts; HN users in Feb 2026 said 2.0 does not hold together much beyond 15 seconds; and 2.5's 30s claim is officially made but UNVERIFIED in practice. Plan 10-15s takes and a high reject rate. Hold identity with a reference pack - a composite turnaround sheet plus a lighting board - rather than by extending duration; 2.5 accepts 30 image / 50 total references, which is what that capacity is for. Use 2.0 Mini (20 credits per 8s vs 36) as the cheap iteration path for blocking, then re-run the keeper on the full model.
Determine the reliable length yourself: generate at 4, 8, 12, 20, 30s with identical conditioning, embed every frame with a face-recognition model, plot cosine similarity to frame 0, and set take length just before similarity declines.
remediation_playbook.risk: Over-cutting produces a jumpy edit that fights a talking-head's intimacy. Cutting mid-word or mid-gesture is jarring. If takes are generated independently, continuity errors appear across the cut - hair, clothing, hand position, background objects and lighting must match, which is exactly where independently-generated takes fail. Use consistent conditioning across takes and check continuity at every cut. Also note the distribution-side risk from forensic-23: heavily templated multi-take output at scale is precisely what Meta's unoriginal-content and YouTube's inauthentic-content policies target, so vary genuinely rather than mass-producing from one template.

remediation_playbook.how:
START HERE: [MEASURED] generate_audio defaults to TRUE on every Seedance model and the model invented spoken dialogue your prompt never scripted. If you are dubbing your own VO, set generate_audio=false explicitly - otherwise you are paying for and shipping synthetic speech, plus possible spontaneous subtitles and background music (vendor-admitted for 2.0).
If you keep or replace the audio, a clean voice over a silent room is something a phone at arm's length physically cannot produce. [MEASURED] your source has 77% of energy below 1 kHz, very weak HF air, and ~29% of frames at near-digital-silence between phrases - no room tone at all.
  1. Add a continuous room-tone bed at roughly -50 to -45 dBFS. Use a genuine recording, not synthesised noise, longer than the clip so it never loops audibly.
  2. Convolve the voice with a short impulse response matched to the visible room (small reverberant space, RT60 ~0.3-0.5s), mixed low.
  3. Model the phone mic: high-pass around 80 Hz, low-pass around 14 kHz, and light compression, since phone mics AGC hard.
  4. Match the encode lineage: your file arrives at AAC-LC 44.1 kHz stereo ~132 kbps, while Meta's Reels spec asks for AAC-LC 128 kbps+ at 48 kHz stereo. Resample yourself: `-c:a aac -b:a 192k -ar 48000 -ac 2` on the master.
ffmpeg sketch:
  ffmpeg -i video.mp4 -i roomtone.wav -filter_complex \
    "[0:a]highpass=f=80,lowpass=f=14000,acompressor=threshold=-18dB:ratio=3[v]; \
     [1:a]volume=-48dB[r];[v][r]amix=inputs=2:duration=first" \
    -c:v copy -c:a aac -b:a 192k -ar 48000 out.mp4
Also check lip-sync lag stability across the clip - accumulating drift is a clear generative signature, best fixed by shorter takes (rem-13).
remediation_playbook.risk: Too much room tone sounds like a bad recording and hurts retention, which matters more commercially than any forensic concern. Too much reverb makes the voice distant and unintelligible on phone speakers, where most Reels are consumed. Over-compression flattens delivery. And if your reverb does not match the visible room - a big hall sound in a small bedroom - you have replaced one inconsistency with a more noticeable one.

remediation_playbook.how:
Order changes the result substantially and several plausible orderings are wrong. Recommended pipeline:
  1. Generate at 1080p (not 720p), generate_audio=false if dubbing, in 10-15s takes.
  2. Photometric first: exposure/clipping (rem-07), then AE/WB drift (rem-08). These must precede grain, because applying them after would scale the grain and decorrelate it from the luma profile you calibrated.
  3. Lens geometry (rem-05: distortion, CA, vignette, veiling glare) - anchored to the lens, so before any frame motion.
  4. Motion: shake crop + rotate (rem-03), rolling-shutter shear (rem-04), from a padded source.
  5. Frame-rate conform 24->29.97 and motion blur (rem-06, forensic-24) in ONE minterpolate pass, AFTER shake so camera motion contributes to the blur.
  6. Focus hunt (rem-09) and frame-locked smudge (rem-10) - the smudge must come after the shake crop so it stays locked to the frame.
  7. Grain LAST in the visual chain (rem-01), immediately before encoding. Everything above resamples, blurs or averages, all of which would destroy grain applied earlier.
  8. Encode camera master (rem-02 stage 1) with SEI stripping (rem-12).
  9. Container laundering (rem-12).
 10. Upload. For QC only, additionally run rem-02 stage 2 and compare through the harness.
Validated combined chain (steps 3-7 in one ffmpeg invocation):
  ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -f lavfi -i "nullsrc=s=760x1352:r=30" -filter_complex \
   "[0:v]scale=760:1352:flags=lanczos, \
     lenscorrection=k1=-0.028:k2=0.004:i=bilinear, \
     sendcmd=f=shake.cmd,crop=720:1280:20:36,rotate=angle=0:fillcolor=none:bilinear=1, \
     curves=master='0/0.004 0.18/0.176 0.5/0.5 0.78/0.802 0.9/0.918 0.97/0.962 1/0.978', \
     vignette=angle=PI/7,chromashift=cbh=1:crh=-1,unsharp=5:5:-0.25:5:5:0[v]; \
    [1:v]format=gray,noise=alls=40:allf=t+u,format=yuv420p,scale=720:1280[g]; \
    [v][g]blend=all_expr='A+(B-128)*(0.06*(0.5+1.5*pow(1-A/255,1.2)))'" \
   -c:v libx264 -profile:v high -preset slow -b:v 16M -pix_fmt yuv420p prod.mp4
 [MEASURED] this exact command runs and outputs 720x1280. Swap the blend weight for the inverted-U form from rem-01 once you have calibrated K.
remediation_playbook.risk: The cumulative softening is the thing to watch: scale, lens resample, rotate, motion blur, focus blur and negative unsharp all remove high-frequency energy, and stacking all of them will push your FFT slope well past the target and make the clip look soft at 1 Mbps. Measure after every added stage rather than only at the end. Applying grain anywhere but last is the single most common ordering mistake and silently wastes the calibration. Each intermediate write should be at CRF 10 or lossless - intermediate re-encodes at CRF 20+ stack generation loss and add encode signatures you did not intend.
